pages.transcription:
4.II.41
Dear Hanna u. Manfred,
I'll have to be a little shorter to-day as we have
to go out very soon. Fortunately I have written you almost everything so
that I need not add much. Our telegram to-day gave you Eva's address:
Amity Hall
Mount Airy Road
Croton-on-Hudson
New York.
We took her up there to-day - that is to say we went to New Rochelle and
Mr. Salmon took us over to Croton in his car, waited until I had been at
the school, discussed all the arrangements with Mrs. Schaeffer, and then
took us back to New York. I believe I wrote you all about Mrs. Schaeffer
in my last letter. The house, as Stefan writes, is beautifully situated
with large grounds, but it is very plainly furnished and run on very simple
lines. It is a little on the primitive side (but has good windows and
centralheating) but I do not think Eva will miss anything. The food is
plain and good - I had lunch there twice - and as to company there should
be several among fifteen children between 3 and 14 years of age. That she
will have to choose herself, I did not see more than one or two children,
as most of them were at school.
As to school, we decided for the Hessian Hill School,
a rather progressive private school, that means a lot of independent and
private work if I understood it right. I was a little hesitant at first,
as I am beginning to get oldfashioned, but it was recommended from various
sides as an excellent school with only very good staff. So Eva will go
there to-morrow and the day after as visitor and will get to know it. Mrs.
Sch. who has 13 of her 15 children in that school warned me that probably
it would take a week for her to adapt herself to that different way of
learnin and teaching. But she says that it has an excellent influence
on the children, and she is very sensible, normal and not at all verstiegen
in her views, and I trust her opinion. Also Stefan had a very good impression
of her, and he knows her husband since many years. - I'll phone Eva in a
few days to see how she feels in the new and completely different surroun-
dings - imagine the contrast between Salmon's house where she had all the
attention and could do what she wanted and had every wish granted and a nice
but very modest home with fifteen children. But I hope she will feel at
home there very quickly and like the change.
As to Salmon's I must say that they behaved very decently;
Mr. S. seems to have overdone his efforts to gain her love and confidence and
in some strange reaction she does not care very much for him although she
likes them both. But Mr. S. really felt sorry at her leaving and immediate-
ly arranged with Mrs. Sch. that Eva should spend the first free weekend -
they are allowed to go away for the weekend once a month,but can have visitors
every Saturday and Sunday and go out with them for the day - again at his
house.He is quite determined that the ~~xxxx~~ relationship shall not be at an
end, and maybe that they will understand each other better when they are not
always together. Of Mrs. Salmon too I had again not a bad impression. She
is much cooler and reserved than her husband, but as I myself am not too
effusive towards people I hardly know, I hm not the one to blame her for it.
On the whole I believe Eva will be more satisfied in her new surroundings in
spite of the fact that at S.'s she was spoilt and could do whatever she felt
like doing.
As to music lessons, the Hessian Hill School is supposed
to have very good teachers, and she can take her lessons there. There is a
piano at Schaeffer's although not a grand piano and I am afraid, even not a
very good one.
I hope you are well and follow our request and go to
Bath now for some months, I both of you. Kindest regards, best love Lotte

Thanks for your letter of jan 13th which we received two days ago.
